statement: Some odd positive integers, not necessarily different, add up to $20$. What is the largest possible value of their product?

choices.misconception: I used five 3s, which add up to $15$, and forgot to use the remaining $5$.
I used four 5s, which add up to $20$, but 3s give a bigger product than 5s for the same total.
I used six 3s to make $18$ and then two 1s for the last $2$. The 1s add nothing to the product, and swapping $3 + 1 + 1$ for a $5$ does better.
I forgot that the numbers must be odd and used ten 2s.

hints: A part equal to 1 uses up some of the sum without helping the product, and big parts can be broken into smaller ones.
Any odd part $p \ge 7$ can be replaced by $3, 3, p - 6$, which makes the product bigger. Also, two 5s can be replaced by $3, 3, 3, 1$, since $27 > 25$.
So the parts are 1s, 3s and at most one 5. Compare the best list with one 5 against the best list with no 5.

solutions.reliable: First, no part needs to be $7$ or more: an odd part $p \ge 7$ can be replaced by the odd parts $3, 3, p - 6$, which keeps the sum and has product $9(p - 6) > p$. So every part is $1$, $3$ or $5$. Next, two 5s can be replaced by $3, 3, 3, 1$, which has the same sum and product $27 > 25$, so there is at most one $5$. With one $5$, the other parts are 3s and 1s adding up to $15$, and the best is five 3s, for a product of $3^5 \cdot 5 = 1215$. With no $5$, the parts are 3s and 1s adding up to $20$, and the best is six 3s and two 1s, for a product of $3^6 = 729$. So the largest product is $1215$, from $3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 20$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
